pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Your friend backs up their project by copying the folder to `project_final_v3`. What can Git do for them that folder copies fundamentally can't?
expected_points: one folder plus a history of labeled snapshots instead of copy sprawl
each commit records who, when, and a message saying why
you can compare any two versions and see exact line-by-line changes
you can rewind to any earlier snapshot reliably

questions.prompt: You edit a file, run `git add` on it, then edit it again. Where do your changes live right now, and what would a commit at this moment contain?
expected_points: the first edit is in the staging area, the second only in the working tree
commit would record the staged version, not the latest saved file
add copies a file's state at that moment; later edits need another add

questions.prompt: Walk me through recording a change to a file, from editing it to it being in history — which commands, in what order, and what does each do?
expected_points: git status shows each file's state and suggests what to do next
git diff shows unstaged line-by-line edits; git diff --staged reviews the draft
git add stages the file; git commit -m seals the snapshot with a message
a good message says what changed and why, not 'wip' or 'fix'

questions.prompt: What is the difference between what `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log` each show you?
expected_points: status: current state of files across working tree and staging area
diff: exact line changes (unstaged by default, --staged for the draft)
log: the chain of past commits with authors, dates, and messages

questions.prompt: Why must build artifacts and secrets stay out of commits, and how does .gitignore keep them out?
expected_points: artifacts are regenerated from source and change every build — pure noise
secrets in a commit stay readable in history forever, even if deleted later
gitignore lists patterns for untracked files git should stop suggesting
it does not untrack files that were already committed

questions.prompt: You committed a password file three commits ago and deleted it in the next commit. `git status` is clean. Is the password safe? What does this tell you about commits?
expected_points: not safe — the old commit still contains it and anyone with the repo can read it
history is append-only; deleting in a new commit doesn't alter old ones
the only reliable protection is never committing the secret at all

questions.prompt: After `git init`, a hidden `.git` folder appears. What lives in there, and what happens to your project if you delete it?
expected_points: the entire history and Git's bookkeeping live in .git
deleting it destroys the history; the working-tree files remain
the folder simply stops being a repository
